newsitem.title: CANADA: Hong Kong's Lee, China's Lu vie for Canada support.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong's Lee, China's Lu vie for Canada support.

text.p: Hong Kong's leading democracy activist and China's top policymaker for the territory lobbied for support in Canada on Thursday, offering sharply different views on the future of the British colony after it reverts to Chinese rule in July.

Lu Ping, director of Beijing's Hong Kong and Macau affairs office, began a cross-country speaking tour in Vancouver while Martin Lee, chairman of the territory's Democratic Party, met Prime Minister Jean Chretien in Ottawa.
Lee criticised Canada's decision not to support a United Nations resolution condemning Beijing's human rights record.
"It gives the world, including China, the wrong message, that Canada seems to be in doubt about her commitment to support of democracy and human rights for the rest of the world," Lee said in Ottawa.

A British colony for more than 150 years, Hong Kong returns to China on July 1 and democracy activists have sought to raise alarm abroad over China's plans to curb some civil rights and roll back democracy in the territory.
Lee, who is scheduled to meet U.S. President Bill Clinton on Friday, is on an international tour to bolster support for Hong Kong's democracy movement before the handover.
Vowing to stay in Hong Kong and continue to fight for civil liberties after July, Lee accused China of violating an agreement to maintain democracy in Hong Kong.
He urged Canada and the United States to tell "Chinese leaders that they must adhere to their promises made to the people of Hong Kong and implicitly to the rest of the world."

In Vancouver, Lu assured a business audience that China will live up to its promises to grant Hong Kong a high degree of autonomy and said its people will have more influence over their fate than under British rule.
"Hong Kong people will have a larger role in determining their own future, will be in control of their own destiny and will be able to determine their own success," he said.

The period after July will be looked upon as the time "when Hong Kong people truly became masters of their own destiny." He repeated a pledge to hold elections for a new Hong Kong legislature in the first half of 1998 to replace a provisional Chinese-appointed body.
He said a plan to require that Hong Kong residents obtain police permission before holding demonstrations did not mean political demonstrations would be banned.
Diplomats have described Lu's tour as an eleventh-hour gesture by Beijing to lobby the West after publicity over visits by Hong Kong democrats including Lee.
Asked by reporters about Lee's meeting on Friday with Clinton, Lu uttered a firm "no comment."
The main message of Lu's visit is to reassure Canada that the transition to Chinese rule will be smooth and Hong Kong will a stable place for foreigners to invest.
Lu met briefly with Canadian Foreign Affairs Minister Lloyd Axworthy and was due to visit Toronto on Friday before heading to Ottawa for more substantial talks with Axworthy.
